fields.explanation: The challenged arithmetic statement quantifies integer d>1. At d=2 its value is6/2^(2^1)=6/4=3/2, so it is not less than1. For every integer d>=3, 2^(d-1)>=4 and the denominator is at least16, so the numerical inequality does hold. Thus d=2 is the unique exception in the stated integer range. The selected rational theorem certifies the d=2 counterexample. Correcting this numerical range alone does not validate the other probabilistic steps of the attempted Ramsey proof.
fields.flaw: The proof asserts that the union-bound quantity binom(4,2)*(1/2)^{2^{d-1}} = 6/2^{2^{d-1}} is strictly less than 1 for all d > 1; this inequality is what the conclusion (P(X) < 1, hence a monochromatic Q_d exists with positive probability) rests on.
fields.problem: Prove that $R(Q_d) \leq 2^{3d}$, where $R(Q_d)$ is the Ramsey number of the $d$-dimensional hypercube $Q_d$.
fields.source_context:
0001 | I want to try a probabilistic proof for this problem. Please give some comments on this attempt at a proof.
0002 | 
0003 | Let $G$ be our complete graph $K_{2^{3d}}$, with the edges colored red/blue randomly and independently. My observation is that, any $d$-dimensional cube $Q_d$ can be constructed from $2$ copies of $Q_{d-1}$, with the missing edges added appropriately. Since $2^{3d} = 2^{3(d-1)}\cdot 8$, by induction $G$ contains $8$ copies of monochromatic $Q_{d-1}$, at least $4$ of which must be of the same color (wlog let the color be red).
0004 | 
0005 | Now consider the event $X$ that none of the pair of $Q_{d-1}$ among those $4$ copies form a monochromatic red $Q_d$. This is the union of the events that all pairs of $Q_{d-1}$ are invalid. By the union bound, we have:
0006 | $$\mathbb{P}(X) \leq \sum \mathbb{P} \text{(the pair of $Q_{d-1}$ forms invalid $Q_d$)} = {4 \choose 2} \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{2^{d-1}} = \frac{6}{2^{2^{d-1}}} < 1, \text{ for $d>1$.}$$
0007 | 
0008 | Hence the probability that one of the pair of $Q_{d-1}$ forms a valid, monochromatic red $Q_d$ is strictly positive.
0009 | 
0010 | —————————————  
0011 | **Edit:** I’m putting up a bounty for this question. Hints or answers would be appreciated.
fields.witness: d = 2 (an integer with d > 1, hence inside the asserted range). At d = 2 the exponent is 2^(d-1) = 2^1 = 2, so 2^(2^(d-1)) = 2^2 = 4, and binom(4,2)*(1/2)^(2^(d-1)) = 6/4 = 3/2. The claim says this quantity is < 1; here it equals 3/2 > 1 (equivalently, numerator 6 > denominator 4). It is the unique integer counterexample: for every integer d >= 3 the exponent 2^(d-1) >= 4, so 2^(2^(d-1)) >= 16 > 6 and the inequality does hold.
